passage:
For three months I complained about Raghav at every chai break. He ran the lab booking sheet, and somehow my team kept losing our slots to his. I'd say, "He's doing it on purpose," and people would nod. It felt good for about ten minutes. Then I noticed Raghav had stopped saying good morning to me. Word travels.
So I did it differently. I went through the booking sheet and noted every slot we'd lost since June, fourteen in all, with dates. I asked our lab manager for a meeting on a Monday morning, not in the middle of a deadline. I said, "Here's the pattern. I'm not saying anyone did it deliberately. Could we try a rota instead of first-come booking?"
The manager agreed to test it for a month. Raghav even helped design it. I also owed him an apology for those chai breaks. When I finally said sorry last week, he laughed: "Took you long enough, Chetan."

qa.q: How many slots had the team lost since June?
qa.a: Fourteen in all, noted with dates.

qa.q: Why did Chetan decide to change approach?
qa.a: Chetan felt uneasy and guilty after noticing Raghav had stopped saying good morning, seeing that the venting had spread and hurt their relationship.

qa.q: What made Chetan's complaint effective?
qa.a: It had evidence, fourteen dated slots, good timing on a Monday morning, went to the lab manager, avoided blame, and proposed a rota.

qa.q: How might the chai-break venting have looked from Raghav's side?
qa.a: Raghav probably heard he was being called deliberately unfair behind his back and felt hurt or defensive, which is why he stopped saying good morning.

grounding: A young professional moves from venting behind a colleague's back to raising the complaint with evidence, good timing and a proposed fix through the proper channel.

passage:
"Honestly, the people working from home just aren't pulling their weight," Kalyani said, reaching for a samosa. "Everyone knows it."
Dilnaz put down her cup. She worked from home three days a week. "Kalyani, I disagree with that."
"Oh, I didn't mean you—"
"It's okay, I'm not taking it personally. I just don't think the numbers say that. Our home-based team closed more tickets last quarter than the office team. The report's on the shared drive."
Kalyani frowned. "Maybe. But they never pick up when I call."
"That's fair, and worth fixing. Maybe it's about how we reach each other, not where people sit. What if we agreed on core hours when everyone answers calls?"
Kalyani chewed slowly. "Core hours. Hmm. I could live with that."
"I'll suggest it at Monday's meeting. Want to present it with me?"
"Okay. But I'm still checking that report."

qa.q: Where is the report?
qa.a: The report's on the shared drive.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have been feeling when she said "I didn't mean you"?
qa.a: Kalyani was likely a little embarrassed and defensive, realising Dilnaz worked from home.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz keep the challenge firm but not hostile?
qa.a: She said plainly that she disagreed, pointed to evidence, accepted Kalyani's fair point about calls, and proposed core hours and presenting them together. 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Dilnaz had snapped back angrily?
qa.a: Kalyani would likely have dug in to defend her claim, and they would not have landed on core hours together.

grounding: A young adult challenges a colleague's claim directly and respectfully, focusing on the issue and evidence, which leaves room for the other to shift.

passage:
Monday night
Today in the review Mehak told the whole room the launch slipped because "Ojas never sent the test results." I sent them on the 3rd. I have the email.
The reply in my head was pure poison: "Maybe try opening your inbox, Mehak." My jaw actually hurt from holding it in. I said only, "I'll check the timeline and follow up," and wrote down her exact words.
After the meeting I did three things. Found the email from the 3rd, with the attachment and her reply, "thanks, got it." Wrote a short, dated note of what was said in the room. Sent both to our manager with one line: "Could we correct the record, and agree on how test results are handed over?"
No sarcasm. No group chat. Still furious, honestly. But tomorrow I'll be the one with the facts, not the one who started a fight.

qa.q: When were the test results sent?
qa.a: The test results were sent on the 3rd.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when Mehak shifted the blame in the review?
qa.a: Ojas felt furious and wronged, with a sarcastic reply ready and a jaw that hurt from holding it in.

qa.q: What three steps did Ojas take after the meeting?
qa.a: Found the email from the 3rd with Mehak's "thanks, got it" reply, wrote a dated note of what was said, and sent both to the manager asking to correct the record and agree on handovers.

qa.q: What would change if Ojas had answered with sarcasm in the room?
qa.a: The review would have turned into a public fight, and Ojas might have looked like the aggressor instead of the one with the facts.

grounding: Facing public blame, a young professional keeps to facts, avoids a public rebuttal, documents events and escalates through the manager instead of retaliating with sarcasm.

passage:
Secretary's note, residents' committee, 12 May
The hall dispute came up again. Vandana's morning yoga group wants the hall from 6 to 8 every day. The senior citizens' carrom club says they've used it at 7 for fifteen years. Voices were rising; Mr. Iyer said he had never been so insulted.
Sachin, our youngest member, asked if he could suggest something. He began, "Both groups want the same thing, really: the hall full and people healthy." Then: "What if yoga runs from 6 to 7:15 and carrom from 7:30, as a one-month trial? We review it at the June meeting. And the yoga group sets up the carrom boards before they leave."
Vandana said the club had been generous to share. Mr. Iyer said the yoga people had been patient. Both said yes to the trial.
I'd like Sachin to chair the June review.

qa.q: How long had the carrom club used the hall at 7?
qa.a: They had used it at 7 for fifteen years.

qa.q: What was Mr. Iyer feeling before Sachin spoke?
qa.a: Mr. Iyer felt deeply insulted and angry, saying he had never been so insulted.

qa.q: What made Sachin's proposal easy for both sides to accept?
qa.a: He began from a shared goal, offered a split schedule as a one-month trial with a review, and gave the yoga group a helpful role, so nobody lost face. 👍

qa.q: How did Vandana respond to the trial?
qa.a: Vandana acknowledged that the club had been generous to share and agreed to the trial.

grounding: A young adult proposes a middle path framed around shared goals, a trial period and acknowledged concessions, which lets both sides keep dignity.

passage:
Counsellor's note, alumni career desk, Wednesday
Disha, a recent graduate, came in today with her friend Aditi. Disha's new employer wants her to sign a two-year service bond by tonight. The recruiter told her, "Don't show this to your parents, they won't understand the startup world," and said the offer "disappears at midnight."
Aditi had persuaded her to come. Disha said Aditi's words were, "I think you should get it checked, but it's your call. I'll come with you if you want."
We talked about the difference: Aditi gave a reason and left the choice with Disha. The recruiter used a deadline, secrecy and cutting her off from family.
Disha looked relieved and a bit shaken. Next steps, today: she emailed the company asking for a week to review, and I referred her to the university's legal aid cell for the bond clause. I'll call her on Friday.

qa.q: When did the recruiter say the offer would disappear?
qa.a: The offer "disappears at midnight."

qa.q: How did Disha feel after the talk at the career desk?
qa.a: Disha felt relieved and a bit shaken, seeing that the recruiter's pressure was a warning sign.

qa.q: What steps were taken the same day?
qa.a: Disha emailed the company asking for a week to review, and the counsellor referred her to the university's legal aid cell for the bond clause.

qa.q: How was Aditi's influence different from the recruiter's?
qa.a: Aditi gave a reason and left the choice with Disha, offering to come along, while the recruiter used a deadline, secrecy and isolation from family.

grounding: Honest persuasion leaves the right to say no, while a deadline, secrecy and isolation from family are warning signs of coercion to discuss with trusted people.

passage:
Ganga had prepared for the call with Shreya from HR the way she used to prepare for exams: a page of notes on her desk in the Bengaluru flat. Three projects she had led. What two friends in similar roles had said about pay. A range she could live with.
When Shreya named the offer, it was below the bottom of Ganga's range. Her heart raced. The old Ganga would have said, "Okay, thank you," and cried later.
"Thank you, I'm excited about the role," she said instead. "Based on the projects I've led and what similar roles pay, I was hoping for something higher." She named her range, then stopped talking.
The silence stretched. Shreya said the salary band was fixed this year.
"I understand. Could we look at other parts, a review at six months, or two days a week from home?"
Shreya paused. "The six-month review I can do. Let me check the rest."

qa.q: What was on Ganga's page of notes?
qa.a: Three projects she had led, what two friends in similar roles had said about pay, and a range she could live with.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel when Shreya named the offer?
qa.a: Ganga felt nervous and disappointed, heart racing, since the offer was below her range.

qa.q: What could someone in Ganga's place consider when the salary band is fixed?
qa.a: Asking about other terms, as Ganga did, such as an earlier review or working from home, and talking the offer over with a trusted mentor before deciding.

qa.q: How might Shreya have seen Ganga's approach?
qa.a: Shreya likely saw a prepared, respectful candidate, which may be why she agreed to the six-month review and offered to check the rest.

grounding: A young professional prepares evidence, names a range, listens and asks about non-salary terms instead of accepting silently or pushing aggressively.

passage:
The client demo was at ten the next morning, and at 6 pm Nikita was still staring at a data model she didn't understand. Everyone else on the floor was packing up. On Monday she had told Saurabh, "Sure, I've done this before." She hadn't, not like this.
She could stay all night and hope. Or she could say it.
Her hands were cold as she knocked on his cabin door. "Saurabh, I need to tell you something before it becomes your problem at ten tomorrow. I overstated my experience with this kind of model. I've done the charts and the summary. The join between the two sales tables is where I'm stuck. If Farida can give me thirty minutes tonight, I think I can finish by nine."
Saurabh looked at her for a moment. "Thanks for telling me now and not at 9:55." He picked up the phone. "Farida, can you spare half an hour?"

qa.q: What time was the client demo?
qa.a: The client demo was at ten the next morning.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling as she knocked on Saurabh's door?
qa.a: Nikita felt nervous and ashamed, hands cold, having overstated her experience, but determined not to let it grow into a bigger problem.

qa.q: What made Nikita's admission likely to build trust?
qa.a: She said it early, owned the overstatement, showed what she had finished, named the exact problem, and proposed a plan with Farida's help.

qa.q: How did Saurabh see Nikita's timing?
qa.a: Saurabh appreciated it, thanking her for telling him now rather than at 9:55, and called Farida at once.

grounding: A young professional admits a gap to her manager early and with a plan, which builds trust rather than risking a failed demo.

passage:
Tuesday, first week. Over tea in the canteen, Arnab told Pallavi he had lost his job and hadn't told his family. "Please keep it to yourself." She listened, didn't offer to fix his CV, didn't tell anyone. "Thank you for trusting me," she said.
Monday, the week after. Arnab called late, voice flat. He hadn't eaten properly in days. Then: "Honestly, nobody would notice if I just disappeared."
Pallavi's stomach went cold. "Arnab, I'm really glad you told me. I'm worried about your safety, and this is one thing I can't keep secret." She stayed on the line, called a helpline with him on speaker, and then, with his okay, rang his elder brother, who drove over that same night.
Saturday, two weeks later. Arnab met her outside the counsellor's clinic. "You broke my secret," he said, and then, "I'm glad you did."

qa.q: What did Arnab ask Pallavi in the canteen?
qa.a: He asked, "Please keep it to yourself."

qa.q: What did Pallavi feel when Arnab said nobody would notice if he disappeared?
qa.a: Pallavi felt alarmed and frightened for his safety; her stomach went cold.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do that night, and why was it right?
qa.a: She told Arnab she couldn't keep this secret, stayed on the line, called a helpline with him and rang his elder brother, because his safety mattered more than confidentiality.

qa.q: How did Arnab come to see the broken secret?
qa.a: At first he felt his trust had been broken, but two weeks later, outside the counsellor's clinic, he said he was glad she did it.

grounding: A young adult receiving a confidence listens without judging or fixing, keeps it private, but breaks confidentiality the same night when the friend's safety is at risk.

subtype: Reading humour across cultures and settings [Mismatch]
passage:
"Oh, look who decided to grace us!" Zeenat called out as Disha slipped into the meeting room ten minutes late. A few people laughed.
Disha sat down without a word, face stiff.
After the meeting, Zeenat caught up with her at the printer. "Hey, you went very quiet. Was it the joke?"
"It was in front of the whole team. I was late because the metro stopped for forty minutes."
"Oh no. Disha, I'm sorry. At my old office in Leeds, that line was just how we said hello to latecomers. Everyone teased everyone."
"Here it sounds like you're calling me out. In my family, teasing is for people you're very close to."
Zeenat nodded slowly. "That's fair. We don't know each other well yet."
"No."
"So, new rule for me: I joke about myself, or about this printer." She kicked it gently. "Never about someone's lateness."
Disha finally smiled. "The printer deserves it."

qa.q: Why was Disha late?
qa.a: The metro stopped for forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when she sat down without a word?
qa.a: Disha felt embarrassed and hurt, since the teasing came in front of the whole team when she was late for a real reason.

qa.q: What new rule did Zeenat set, and why does it help?
qa.a: Joke about herself or the printer, never about someone's lateness, because inclusive humour doesn't single anyone out.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat expect the line to land as friendly?
qa.a: At her old office in Leeds that line was just how people greeted latecomers and everyone teased everyone, so she meant it as a hello.

grounding: Teasing that is friendly in one workplace can seem rude in another, so a young professional keeps humour inclusive and watches reactions.

passage:
At the Friday team lunch, one of the sales team held up Ritu's new ID photo on his phone. "Ritu's new look! Very... mushroom." The table laughed. Ritu laughed too, a short sound, and pulled her dupatta closer.
Divyansh didn't laugh. "Nah, that one's not fair. The ID camera makes everyone look like a suspect. Mine looks like I've just been arrested."
He held up his own. The table laughed harder, at him this time, and the phone went down.
Later, near the lift, Ritu said quietly, "Thanks. I laughed because what else do you do."
"I know. That's why I said something. Laughing along doesn't mean it's okay with you."
"Some days I don't mind jokes. Just not about how I look."
"Noted. I'll stick to bad ID photos of myself and the office coffee."
She smiled properly this time. "Deal."

qa.q: What did the sales colleague call Ritu's new look?
qa.a: He called it "Very... mushroom."

qa.q: What did Ritu's short laugh and pulling her dupatta closer suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Ritu felt uncomfortable and self-conscious, laughing only because she didn't know what else to do.

qa.q: How did Divyansh shift the joke without starting a fight?
qa.a: He said it wasn't fair, then turned the humour on his own ID photo, so the table laughed at him and the phone went down.

qa.q: How did the rest of the table seem to read Ritu's laugh?
qa.a: They seemed to take it as her being fine with the joke, since she laughed too, missing the signs of discomfort.

grounding: A young professional avoids jokes about a colleague's appearance and responds when she looks uncomfortable, since laughing along does not prove she is okay with it.
